confidence_note: Book text not read. Verified through book summaries and talks: the three forces Abundance, Asia, Automation; the argument that logical left-brain work is increasingly done cheaper abroad or by software, while empathy, design, story and meaning rise in value; Pink's own caveat that the left/right split is a simplified metaphor. A tax-return example (work done in India, software like TurboTax) appears in secondhand summaries; no figures are used. The reference's claims about AI reading contracts and about 1990s 'safest jobs' are not Pink's (2005) and were NOT used. Added: Conceptual Age, L/R-directed thinking and the meaning of symphony are standard Pink terms, not checked against the text.
facts: Pink argues that three forces are shifting which skills pay: Abundance, Asia and Automation.
Abundance: most people in rich countries can buy plenty cheaply, so design, meaning and beauty matter.
Asia: routine white-collar work, such as preparing tax returns, can be done abroad at lower cost.
Automation: software now handles routine, rule-based analysis.
Pink calls the left hemisphere's logical, sequential style 'left-brain' and argues the right-brain style (big picture, empathy) now needs equal weight.
He names six 'senses': design, story, symphony, empathy, play, meaning.
Pink acknowledges the left/right brain split is a simplified metaphor for two styles of thinking.
Pink says the Information Age, which rewarded logical, linear workers such as lawyers, accountants and programmers, is giving way to what he calls the Conceptual Age.
Pink calls the two modes L-directed and R-directed thinking, and says the three forces raise the value of the second without removing the first.
Symphony, in Pink's list, is the ability to see the big picture and put pieces together.
scene_details: A tax return prepared overseas or by software
Three words on a page: Abundance, Asia, Automation
tension: The skills that were safest for a professional are the ones easiest to send abroad or hand to software.
opening_idea: Start with the tax return: the same form done by an accountant at home, an accountant abroad and a piece of software.

lessons.idea: Skills that follow fixed rules are easiest to copy elsewhere or automate; add judgment about people to the work you do.
lessons.anchor: Pink's three forces, Abundance, Asia and Automation, each take routine analysis out of local hands.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A bookkeeper who also explains numbers to a worried shop owner offers something a form cannot.

reflect_final: Which part of your own work is routine enough for software, and which part depends on understanding a particular person?

use_cases.situation: Your team debates what to automate.
use_cases.move: Pink's Automation force takes routine analysis first. List which tasks follow fixed rules and which need judging a person.

use_cases.situation: A friend fears for their job.
use_cases.move: Ask which part of their day needs someone who understands the customer.

use_cases.situation: You plan what to learn next.
use_cases.move: Pick one skill about people, like listening or explaining, and practise it in one conversation.

pocket_idea: Pink's three forces move routine analysis abroad or into software; invest in the part of your work that needs understanding a person.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: In Pink's argument, a tax return can be done abroad or by software, but understanding the client is harder to ship.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Daniel Pink says three forces, Abundance, Asia and Automation, are changing which skills pay. Rule-based work can be done cheaper abroad or by software, and with plenty to buy, design and meaning matter more. He adds that left and right brain is a simplified metaphor.
